title: Buddha Seated on the Coils of a Naga

image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Gift of Alexander M. Polsky, 1988
image.license: Public domain. Released under Creative Commons Zero (CC0) through the Met's Open Access program

altText: A very small bronze figure of the Buddha seated on the coiled body of a naga, a serpent. The sculpture is about the size of a matchbox and has a dark metal surface.

source.verifiedBy: Met Collection API object record (title, date, medium, culture, classification, tags Buddhism, Buddha, public-domain flag, image URLs, credit line) and the Met catalog page (period and dimensions)

context: A tiny bronze of the Buddha seated on the coils of a naga, or serpent, made in the Angkor period in the first quarter of the 12th century. The Met gives its place of origin as Cambodia or Thailand. It is only about 11.3 cm tall. The record has no label text, but the title matches a well-known Buddhist story in which a naga shelters the Buddha.

descriptions.k: This tiny bronze shows the Buddha sitting on a big snake. The snake is called a naga. Its body is coiled up like a cushion. The statue is only as big as your hand. Why would a snake help the Buddha?
descriptions.g12: In an old Buddhist story, a giant snake called a naga protects the Buddha from a storm. This tiny bronze shows the Buddha sitting on the naga's coiled body. It is only about 11 centimeters tall, and it is about 900 years old. How does the naga help the Buddha sit up high?
descriptions.g35: This small bronze, about 11 centimeters tall, shows the Buddha seated on the coils of a naga, a serpent in Southeast Asian stories. Artists in Cambodia or Thailand made it around the early 1100s. A well-known Buddhist story tells how a naga sheltered the Buddha during a storm while he meditated. How does the coiled body make a seat? What does the pose suggest?
descriptions.g68: A naga is a serpent being in Indian and Southeast Asian traditions. In a famous Buddhist story, a naga shelters the Buddha during a storm as he meditates, and this small Angkor-period bronze, made around the early 12th century in Cambodia or Thailand, matches that subject. The coils form a seat that lifts the Buddha up. At only about 11 cm tall, how does the sculptor give a tiny figure such stability and importance?
descriptions.g910: This Angkor-period bronze, made in Cambodia or Thailand in the early 12th century, shows the Buddha seated on the coils of a naga. The subject echoes a Buddhist story in which a naga shelters the Buddha during meditation, though the record gives no label text. The coiled base forms a pedestal and symbol at once. At only about 11.3 cm, the work condenses protection, stillness, and power into a hand-sized form. How do composition and scale create that effect?
descriptions.g1112: The image of a Buddha enthroned on naga coils is widely associated with Angkor-period Buddhism, in which serpents are both protectors and bearers of royal and divine status. This small bronze, with its stack of coils supporting a meditating figure, uses the base as an expressive element rather than mere support. The Met's attribution to Cambodia or Thailand reflects the shared artistic world of the Khmer realm and its borderlands. Consider how scale, material, and iconography relate, and how much we can claim without a label or documented context.

k.daily: The Buddha sits on a snake that is coiled up like a cushion. How do you think that feels?
k.emotion: Does the Buddha look worried or calm sitting on the snake? Show us the face you see.
k.observation: Find the Buddha and the coils of the naga. Point to each one.
k.analysis: What part of this tiny statue do you look at first? Why?
k.line: Trace the round coils of the snake with your finger. Do they go up, down, or around?
k.shape: The coils of the snake make round shapes. What do they remind you of?
k.color: The statue is bronze, a dark golden-brown metal. What other things are that color?
k.texture: Snakes can feel smooth, but this one is metal. How do you think the coils feel?
k.space: The Buddha sits high up on top of the snake's body. Why might that be a good place to sit?
k.light: Where does the metal look the brightest? Where does it look the darkest?
k.meaning: In the story, the snake protects the Buddha. Who or what protects you?
k.culture: This statue was made in Cambodia or Thailand about 900 years ago. What stories do you know that have snakes in them?
k.technique: Someone cast this tiny statue in metal. Why might a small statue be easier to carry than a big one?
k.personal: If you could sit on a giant coiled cushion, what would you want it to be made of?
k.critical: Snakes can feel scary in some stories. Why does this snake look different in this one?

g12.daily: The Buddha is sitting on the coils of a naga. What does the artist want us to feel about the naga?
g12.emotion: How does the Buddha's quiet seated pose on top of the coils make you feel? What do you notice that helps?
g12.observation: List four things you can see in this tiny bronze, from the top to the bottom.
g12.analysis: How does the artist guide your eyes from the coils at the bottom up to the Buddha?
g12.line: Follow the curving line of the coils. How do the curves make the base feel strong?
g12.shape: The coils make round, stacked shapes under the Buddha. How do they help the statue feel steady?
g12.color: Bronze is a warm, dark metal. How does the color make the statue feel old?
g12.texture: Which parts of the statue look smooth, and which look like they might have patterns or bumps?
g12.space: The statue is only about 11 centimeters tall. What would it be like to hold something so small and old?
g12.light: Metal catches light on its curves. Where on the coils would the light shine?
g12.meaning: In a Buddhist story, a naga protects the Buddha from a storm. Why might people like stories about protection?
g12.culture: Nagas appear in stories from India and Southeast Asia. Why might different places tell stories about the same creature?
g12.technique: Bronze statues are cast in a mold. What might be hard about casting round coils on a tiny statue?
g12.personal: What is something small you keep that feels very important to you?
g12.critical: The museum does not know exactly where this statue was made. What clues could help figure that out?

g35.daily: The Buddha is shown seated on a naga's coils. How do the coils work as both a seat and a symbol?
g35.emotion: How does the stillness of a seated figure on top of many coils create a feeling of calm and protection?
g35.observation: Take one minute to look at the base and the figure. What small details did you notice after the first look?
g35.analysis: How does the sculptor organize the statue from the wide coiled base to the narrower seated figure?
g35.line: How do the repeating curved lines of the coils compare with the upright line of the seated figure?
g35.shape: How do round shapes in the coils make the base seem strong and steady?
g35.color: How does the dark bronze color affect the mood of the statue?
g35.texture: What can the surface of this old bronze tell you about how it was made and how time has changed it?
g35.space: This statue is small enough to hold. How does its size change how you look at and use it?
g35.light: How might the curves of the coils create highlights and shadows as light moves around the statue?
g35.meaning: In a famous story, a naga shelters the Buddha during a storm. How does this statue tell that story without words?
g35.culture: The Met says this statue is from Cambodia or Thailand. Why might it be hard to say exactly where a very old object was made?
g35.technique: How might a maker create a stack of coils in bronze, and why might that be a good support for a seated figure?
g35.personal: Think of a time someone protected or helped you. How could an artist show that in a small object?
g35.critical: The record gives few details. What can we confidently say about this object, and what should we leave open?

g68.daily: How does the naga's coiled body turn a simple seat into a symbol of protection?
g68.emotion: How does the contrast between the Buddha's stillness and the winding coils create a sense of calm within power?
g68.observation: Describe the figure and its base from bottom to top. Which areas seem most deliberately made?
g68.analysis: How does the broad, coiled base stabilize the composition and focus attention on the seated figure?
g68.line: How do the rhythmic curves of the coils differ from the straighter lines of the seated figure?
g68.shape: How do the stacked round forms of the coils create a pedestal-like shape?
g68.color: How does the dark bronze surface unify the figure and the coils into one form?
g68.texture: How might wear and age affect the way we see the details of the coils and the figure?
g68.space: As a small sculpture in the round, what would you expect to see from the back and the sides?
g68.light: How does the rounded surface of the coils change as light moves around the statue?
g68.meaning: How can a base, like the coils, carry as much meaning as the figure sitting on it?
g68.culture: Angkor-period art blended ideas from Hindu and Buddhist traditions. Why might a naga appear in both?
g68.technique: Why would bronze casting suit a small statue with a complicated base like coils?
g68.personal: What objects in your life act as supports or protectors for something more important?
g68.critical: The origin is given as Cambodia or Thailand. Why do museums sometimes use uncertain labels, and how should we treat them?

g910.daily: How do the coiled naga and seated Buddha together express the idea of protection while meditating?
g910.emotion: How do restraint and symmetry convey serenity in a figure that is also supported by a powerful creature?
g910.observation: Describe the visual hierarchy between figure and base. Which devices keep the Buddha as the focus?
g910.analysis: How does the sculptor integrate the base and the figure so that they read as one unit?
g910.line: How does the repetition of curved lines in the coils create rhythm that contrasts with the figure's stillness?
g910.shape: How do stacked, rounded coils form a stable geometry beneath the seated figure?
g910.color: How does a monochrome bronze surface emphasize form and silhouette, and how might patina have changed it?
g910.texture: What does surface wear suggest about handling, use, or burial?
g910.space: How does the work's hand-sized scale shape ideas about its use, such as personal devotion or portable shrine?
g910.light: How does reflective bronze enhance the sculpture's curves and sense of volume?
g910.meaning: How might a naga symbolize both natural power and protection in Buddhist thought, and how should we handle readings the record does not support?
g910.culture: How does a Buddha on naga coils illustrate the blending of local serpent traditions and Buddhist narratives in Angkor-period art?
g910.technique: What does casting a compact, complex form suggest about the technical skill of Angkor-period bronze workshops?
g910.personal: How do objects meant to be held change your relationship to them compared with large monuments?
g910.critical: How do uncertain attributions such as 'Cambodia or Thailand' reflect the limits of evidence and the history of modern borders?

g1112.daily: What can be argued from the figure and base about protection and authority, and what depends on iconographic knowledge not stated in the record?
g1112.emotion: How does compact, balanced composition create an affect of serenity, and how might viewers differ in their response?
g1112.observation: Describe the sculpture's formal organization with precision. At what point does identification of the story rely on outside knowledge?
g1112.analysis: Analyze how the sculpture merges support and subject so that the base becomes part of the message.
g1112.line: How does the interplay of coiling line and vertical axis structure the sculpture's rhythm and stability?
g1112.shape: How does the tiered geometry of the coils create a symbolic and structural pedestal?
g1112.color: How might patina and age alter our sense of the original bronze surface, and what cannot be reconstructed?
g1112.texture: How should interpreters distinguish casting traces from damage when studying the surface of a small bronze?
g1112.space: How does the sculpture's modest size shape possibilities for handling, display, and ritual use?
g1112.light: How might the reflective qualities of bronze have mattered in intimate devotional settings?
g1112.meaning: How might the figure's relation to the naga communicate protection, kingship, or both, and what evidence would be needed to decide?
g1112.culture: What does the attribution to Cambodia or Thailand suggest about the porous artistic and political boundaries of the Angkor world, and the limits of modern national labels?
g1112.technique: What might the casting of a compact figure-and-coil composition imply about workshop methods, and what remains conjectural?
g1112.personal: How does your relationship with symbols like serpents shape your reading of an image where one is a protector?
g1112.critical: How should viewers weigh a museum's cautious labeling against the desire for a clear story about an object's meaning?

safety.method: Image viewed and approved by the site owner (visual review) on 2026-10-18. Earlier metadata screening: Title, classification (Sculpture), medium (Bronze), culture, and tags (Buddhism, Buddha) checked against the museum record. The catalog page has no label text, so descriptions rely on the title, size, and the well-known Buddhist story of a naga sheltering the Buddha, and they avoid specific claims about the serpent's hood or the Buddha's body. Bare-chested depiction could not be ruled out from metadata alone.

teacherNote.context: A hand-sized bronze (about 11.3 cm) of the Buddha seated on naga coils, Angkor period, first quarter of the 12th century, from Cambodia or Thailand. The Met record provides no label text.
directions: Tell the story of the naga sheltering the Buddha and ask students how the sculpture could tell it without words.
Discuss why museums use labels such as 'Cambodia or Thailand' and what modern borders can hide about older cultures.
Have students sketch the statue from the side and from above and compare.
